facts.statement: The first specimen of Muraenosaurus was collected by Charles E. Leeds and described by H. G. Seeley.
facts.quote: Charles E. Leeds collected the first Muraenosaurus which was then described by H. G. Seeley.

facts.statement: Muraenosaurus lived between 160 and 164 million years ago during the Callovian stage of the Middle Jurassic.
facts.quote: Muraenosaurus grew up to 5.2 m in length and lived roughly between 160 Ma (million years ago) and 164 Ma in the Callovian of the middle Jurassic.

facts.statement: Muraenosaurus was named for its eel-like appearance, characterized by a long neck and small head.
facts.quote: The genus was given its name due to the eel-like appearance of the long neck and small head.

facts.statement: The largest known specimen of Muraenosaurus measured up to 5.2 meters in length.
facts.quote: Muraenosaurus was a medium-sized plesiosaur, with the largest specimen measuring up to 5.2 m long.

facts.statement: Muraenosaurus possessed 66 pre-sacral vertebrae, 44 of which were cervical.
facts.quote: The plesiosaur had 66 pre-sacral vertebrae; 44 of which were cervical.

facts.statement: The coracoids of Muraenosaurus reached widths of nearly 14 inches.
facts.quote: The coracoids reach widths of nearly 14 inches.

facts.statement: The forelimbs of Muraenosaurus were compressed mediolaterally compared to its hind limbs and those of other plesiosaurs.
facts.quote: The forelimb is compressed mediolaterally when compared to the hind limb as well as limbs of other plesiosaurs.

facts.statement: H. G. Seeley initially classified Muraenosaurus in the family Elasmosauridae rather than Cryptoclididae.
facts.quote: When Harry Seeley first described Muraenosaurus it was thought to belong to Elasmosauridae instead of Cryptoclididae.

facts.statement: The similarity between Muraenosaurus and elasmosaurs is now understood as a case of convergent evolution.
facts.quote: However, this is actually a case of convergent evolution between cryptoclidids and elasmosaurs.

facts.statement: Muraenosaurus lived in the shallow, warm Oxford Clay sea, which had an average depth of less than 50 meters.
facts.quote: Muraenosaurus was initially discovered in the Oxford Clay which represents an ancient sea that was both shallow, with an average depth less than 50 meters, and warm (20 °C).

facts.statement: Fossils of Muraenosaurus have been found in the Oxford Clay deposits of southern England and parts of France.
facts.quote: The Oxford Clay deposits are found in southern England and parts of France.

facts.statement: Muraenosaurus likely preyed on teleost fish and cephalopods.
facts.quote: Preferred prey types seem to be teleost fish and cephalopods.

facts.statement: Researchers propose that Muraenosaurus may have fed on benthic fish by floating above them and reaching down with its head.
facts.quote: It is also proposed that species like Muraenosaurus fed upon benthic fishes by floating above them and reaching its head down into the benthos.

facts.statement: Muraenosaurus may have used a benthic grazing strategy to harvest immobile species like cephalopods from the sea floor.
facts.quote: Plesiosauromorphs may also have employed a strategy called benthic grazing where they would harvest relatively immobile species such as cephalopods from the sea floor.

facts.statement: Gastroliths are frequently found in plesiosauromorph stomachs and are associated with this body type.
facts.quote: Gastroliths have often been found within the stomachs of extinct marine reptiles and have been associated with the plesiosauromorph body type.

facts.statement: Muraenosaurus was likely preyed upon by apex predators such as pliosaurs and crocodylomorphs like Liopleurodon and Pliosaurus.
facts.quote: The oceans in the Mesozoic were dominated by pliosaurs and crocodylomorphs (such as Liopleurodon, Pliosaurus, Simolestes, and Metriorhynchus), apex predators that would have preyed upon species like Muraenosaurus.

facts.statement: The original Muraenosaurus specimen may have been damaged due to the casual collection style of Charles Leeds.
facts.quote: The specimen may have suffered some damage due to the casual style of Charles Leeds’ collection.

facts.statement: The first recovered Muraenosaurus specimen was missing pieces of the skull and many caudal vertebrae.
facts.quote: The first muraenosaur was recovered with pieces missing from the skull and many of the caudal vertebrae absent.

facts.statement: Muraenosaurus leedsii is the most complete and only undisputed species within the genus Muraenosaurus.
facts.quote: M. leedsii is the most complete specimen belonging to the genus Muraenosaurus and also the only species that is undoubtedly a member of the genus.

facts.statement: It is debated whether Picrocleidus beloclis should be considered synonymous with Muraenosaurus due to doubts about their relationship.
facts.quote: Picrocleidus beloclis is another plesiosaur originating in the middle Jurassic and found in the Oxford clay formation. Picrocleidus has previously been considered synonymous with Muraenosaurus although there are doubts in the relationship between the two groupings.

facts.statement: It was initially debated that long-necked plesiosaurs were strictly fish-eaters based on their conical teeth.
